Mridul, your Sumit chacha heard "should" more often than his own name. At twenty, in Kanpur, it was every day: "You should do engineering like your brother." "You should marry by twenty-five; the Sharma girl is good." My father said it with love. He carried cement bags so I could study. That made it harder to say no.

I felt I was letting him down just by thinking. Love and pressure on the same plate, every meal.

The turning point was an evening on the roof in mango season. I told him, "Babuji, I respect you more than anyone. I want to study agriculture, not engineering. And I will marry, but not by a date." He didn't speak for two days. Then he asked, "What will you grow?"

I became an agronomist. I married at thirty-one. He danced at the wedding.

Counsellor's note, employee support, 14 May.

Farhan, 25, came in exhausted and guilty. His notebook has a line he reads every morning: "I should be more productive." He says it makes him feel worse, not better; by noon he has usually decided he has failed again.

We worked on the wording. I asked what he wants, not what he should do. He said, "I'd like to finish the client report before lunch." Then we added one concrete step: "Open the report at 9.30 and write the first section."

He looked doubtful. "That's it? No should?"

We agreed he would try the new sentence for a week and note how he feels at noon.

Update, 21 May: he opened the report at 9.30 on five out of five days. He says the guilt is "quieter", and he finished the report on Thursday.

Sharmila

Sunday night

New experiment. For a month my list has said: "I SHOULD exercise. I SHOULD read more. I SHOULD call Amma every day." Every night I look at it and feel like a failure. Then I do none of it and scroll instead.

Pankaj laughed when he saw it. "Your list is shouting at you."

So tonight I rewrote it.
"I'd like to feel stronger. Step: walk to the vegetable market instead of taking an auto, Tuesday and Friday."
"I'd like to read again. Step: ten pages before sleep."
"I'd like Amma to hear from me more. Step: a voice note while the tea boils."

It sounds almost too soft. But reading it, my shoulders don't creep up to my ears. The steps are small enough that I believe them.

Let's see how the week goes.

Yamini

Vaibhav's homework has been too perfect lately. Today he burst into tears when he got one sum wrong. At lunch he told me quietly, "If I get everything right, Mummy and Papa won't fight. They fight because I'm bad at maths."

He said he hears them argue at night about money and "the shop". He said they are kind to him, and nothing suggested anyone is being hurt.

I told him grown-ups argue about grown-up worries, not because of children's marks, and that one wrong sum is completely normal.
This afternoon I shared this with our school counsellor, and we called his mother together. She was upset to hear it and said she and his father will both tell him tonight that it isn't about him. The counsellor will check in with Vaibhav on Monday.

Nitin

qa.q: What does Vaibhav say his parents argue about at night?
qa.a: Vaibhav says they argue about money and "the shop".

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav try so hard to be perfect?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels anxious and responsible, believing his parents fight because of his maths, so being perfect seems like a way to stop it.

qa.q: What did Nitin do the same day?
qa.a: Nitin reassured Vaibhav, shared it with the school counsellor, and called his mother with the counsellor; she agreed to tell him that night it wasn't about him.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's mother feel hearing this?
qa.a: She was upset to learn he had been carrying the blame, and wanted to reassure him that night.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy who believes his parents argue because of his marks and tries to be perfect, and the same-day response.

subtype: Blaming self for parents' arguments [Actor]

Saturday

Mummy and Papa argued again after dinner. I heard "school" and "too much". So it's about me. It's always after my report card, or when I forget my tiffin.

I've decided: from Monday I will be perfect. Up at six. Homework before TV. I won't ask for the new cricket bat. Then they'll be happy.

Ramesh Mama came over this evening and found me on the stairs. I told him my perfect plan. He didn't laugh. He said, "Sid, when my parents argued, I thought it was about me too. It never was. Grown-ups argue about grown-up things. Money, work, tiredness."

Then he went and talked to Mummy. Later Mummy came to my room and said, "We were arguing about Papa's work hours. Not you. Never you."

I'm still getting up at six. But maybe just for cricket.

Siddharth

qa.a: Siddharth heard "school" and "too much".

qa.a: Siddharth felt worried and guilty, sure the arguments were about Siddharth, so being perfect seemed like a way to fix them.

qa.a: He listened without laughing, shared that he had felt the same as a child, explained grown-up arguments, and then told Mummy, who reassured Siddharth that night.

Tuesday night

Charu barely said a word at lunch. She ate half her paratha and looked at her phone. When I told the story about the chemistry teacher's sneeze, she didn't even smile.

All afternoon I was sure it was me. Was it my comment yesterday about her handwriting? Or because I sat with Ravi at assembly? I went over every conversation from the last week like a detective.

By evening I'd written three apology messages and deleted them all.

Then at eight Charu posted: "Our dog Bruno is at the vet, please pray 🙏". Oh. OH.

It had nothing to do with me. I felt relief, and then kind of silly for making her bad day about me.

I sent: "Thinking of you and Bruno. Want to talk?" She replied with a heart.

Suraj

passage:
On the bus back from the district school to their village near Nashik, Dhruv sat with his forehead against the window and didn't say a word to Sonali. Usually he talked the whole way about cricket.

Sonali's mind got busy. Was it because she'd beaten him in the quiz? Because she'd laughed when he dropped his tiffin? Because she'd sat with Meena at lunch? By the third stop she had decided he was angry with her, and her stomach hurt.

At their stop she finally asked, "Dhruv, are you upset with me?"

He looked surprised. "You? No. Baba's buffalo is sick, and the vet can't come till tomorrow. I'm just thinking about her."

Sonali's stomach unknotted, and then she felt a bit silly. "I'm sorry about the buffalo," she said. "Can I come and see her?" Dhruv nodded, almost smiling.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv quiet on the bus?
qa.a: Baba's buffalo was sick, and the vet couldn't come till tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Sonali's stomach hurt by the third stop?
qa.a: Sonali felt anxious and guilty, sure Dhruv's silence was about something she had done.

qa.q: Which choice helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Are you upset with me?" at the stop replaced her worry with the real reason.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling on the bus?
qa.a: Dhruv was worried about the sick buffalo, not thinking about Sonali at all.

grounding: Shows a village girl who assumes a friend's silence on the bus is about her, when he is worried about something else.

The group presentation for the marketing course went badly. The projector died twice, two of the five teammates were down with flu, the professor was in a hurry, and Jaya's competitor-analysis slide had reached the group an hour late, so it went in unchecked.

Grade: C.

Back in the hostel, Jaya lay on her bed. "It's my fault," she messaged Joseph. "My slide was late. I ruined everything for all of you."

Joseph called instead of texting. "Jaya. The projector died twice. Two of us were sick. Nobody rehearsed the ending. Sir cut us off at eight minutes. Your slide was one part."

"But if I'd sent it on time..."

"We'd still have had a dead projector."

Jaya was quiet. She'd been carrying the whole grade on one slide.

qa.a: He listed the other causes, the projector, sick teammates, no rehearsal and being cut off, so her slide became one part, not the whole.

qa.a: Joseph seemed concerned and wanted to correct the picture, which is why he called instead of texting.

The food stall at the Pune college fest had been Ayesha's idea, run with Urmila and three others. It was a flop: they sold barely a third of their samosas. It was the hottest day of the year, their stall was behind the stage speakers, a rival stall sold the same thing cheaper, and the poster Ayesha had designed went up an hour late.

Urmila sat on the floor of their room with a notebook. "Let's list everything that happened." They wrote: heat, location behind the speakers, rival stall, price, late poster.

"That's five things," Urmila said. "Your poster is one. Maybe a small one."

Ayesha looked at the list. It was strange to see her "whole fault" shrink to one line.

subtype: Mapping the share of causes [Response]
passage:
I'm Uday, and when our community library project in Guwahati lost its funding last year, my first thought was: it's all my fault. I had written the grant application. So I must have ruined it.

My co-founder Bidisha didn't argue. She took a paper plate from the kitchen and drew a circle. "Pie chart," she said. "Everything that led to this. Give each thing a slice."

We did it honestly. The funder had cut its budget by half this year: a big slice. Our visitor numbers were low because the building was shut for two months of repairs: another big slice. Our application was two days late and missing one document: my slice. Maybe a fifth.

Looking at the plate, I felt two things. My part was real, and I'd fix it: next time, a checklist and an early deadline. But it was a fifth, not the whole plate. That month we applied to two other funders.

qa.q: What did Bidisha draw the pie chart on?
qa.a: Bidisha drew it on a paper plate.

qa.q: How did Uday feel looking at the finished pie chart?
qa.a: Uday felt steadier: honest about owning a real share, but relieved that it was a fifth, not the whole failure.

qa.q: What did Uday take from the slice that was Uday's own?
qa.a: A checklist and an early deadline for the next application, owning that part and no more.

qa.q: How did Bidisha see the funding loss?
qa.a: Bidisha saw many causes, the budget cut and the closed building, and helped Uday see them too.

grounding: An adult recalls drawing a pie chart of what caused a lost grant, owning their slice and no more.

Mentor's note, architecture practice, 20 September.

Yusuf lost the Kapoor house project this week and came to me convinced it was entirely his fault. "I presented badly. I ruined it."

I asked him to draw a pie chart of every factor. He was reluctant but did it. Slices: the client's budget dropped after a family loss (large); a rival firm offered a faster timeline (medium); our office was short-staffed in August, delaying drawings (medium); his presentation was rushed and he forgot the cost summary (small, about a sixth).

When he looked at it, he said, "So my part is real, but it's a slice." Exactly.

We agreed he will own his slice: he'll practise presentations with me and always end with the cost summary. The other slices I will raise with the partners.

Bhavna

qa.q: What did Yusuf forget in his presentation?
qa.a: Yusuf forgot the cost summary.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when he first came to Bhavna?
qa.a: Yusuf felt guilty and defeated, convinced he alone had ruined the project.

qa.q: How did the pie chart help Yusuf own his part and no more?
qa.a: It showed his rushed presentation as a sixth beside the budget, rival and staffing slices, so he could fix his slice without carrying the whole loss.

qa.q: How might the partners see the other slices?
qa.a: They would likely see issues such as August's short staffing as the office's responsibility, not Yusuf's alone.

Sunday night

The Diwali order disaster. Two hundred sweet boxes for an office party; they arrived an hour late, and forty were crushed. I spent Saturday telling myself it was entirely my fault. I packed the boxes. I booked the tempo.

Kalyani, my partner in the bakery, made me draw a pie chart on the back of an invoice. "Everything that caused it. Be fair."

Slices: the tempo driver got a flat tyre (big). The office changed the delivery time twice (medium). The rain turned the road into a mess (medium). I stacked the boxes too high (mine, maybe a quarter).

A quarter. Not the whole thing. I can own a quarter. From now on, no more than five boxes in a stack, and we keep a backup driver's number.

I still feel bad about the crushed boxes. But the chart let me breathe.

Pema
